lines.text: An island of fire and ice at the edge of the Arctic, with one of the oldest parliaments on Earth and sagas told for a thousand years. This is the story of Iceland.
From about 874, Norse settlers sailed west to an empty island of volcanoes and glaciers, and made it their home.
By around 930 their chieftains met each summer in the open air, reciting the laws and settling disputes. The Althing is often called the oldest parliament still meeting.
They gathered at Thingvellir, a rift valley where the land itself is slowly pulling apart.
Leif Erikson, son of this island world, sailed on beyond Greenland. Around the year one thousand, the sagas say, he reached North America and called it Vinland.
In 1179 Snorri Sturluson was born. He wrote the Prose Edda and the sagas of the Norse kings, and kept the old myths alive.
A century later came Njal's saga, a tale of friendship, feuds and burning, and the greatest of all the Icelandic sagas.
By then Iceland was ruled from Norway, and later Denmark. In 1783 the Laki fissure erupted for eight months, killing the livestock and bringing a terrible famine.
In 1786 Reykjavik became a town, at the very bay where the first settler had made his home.
Halldor Laxness was born in 1902. His novel Independent People told of Iceland's poor farmers, and won him the Nobel Prize.
Vigdis Finnbogadottir, born in 1930, would make history in 1980 as the world's first woman elected president.
In 1944, during the Second World War, Iceland broke its last tie with Denmark and became an independent republic.
Its people lived from the sea, and from 1958 they defended their fishing grounds against Britain in the Cod Wars, and won.
In 1963 a brand new island rose out of the sea off the south coast. Surtsey is left alone, so scientists can watch life arrive by itself.
Two years later Bjork was born, the singer who would carry Iceland's sound around the world.
In 1986 the tall concrete church of Hallgrimskirkja was finished in Reykjavik, shaped like the island's columns of basalt.
That autumn Reagan and Gorbachev met in Reykjavik, and came close to agreeing to scrap all their nuclear weapons.
In 1994 the band Sigur Ros formed, with a soaring, otherworldly sound that seems to come from the landscape itself.
Then in 2008 all three of Iceland's big banks collapsed, and the small nation faced years of hardship.
In April 2010 the volcano Eyjafjallajokull erupted. Its ash closed the skies over Europe for days, and millions of travellers were stranded.
On this young and restless island, the land and its people are still shaping each other.
